title: My friend "Steve Jobs of summer interns" has built another AI game development platform
author: thelionskywalker
selftext:
It all started with my friend Jonas, who’s been called the “Steve Jobs of summer interns”, is very very smart and a machine learning wizard. He’s into gaming and AI, and as soon as [Lovable.dev](http://Lovable.dev) launched, he started wondering: who’s doing the same thing, but for games?  
Pretty quickly, he found [Rosebud.ai](http://Rosebud.ai), which was… ok 😄 so he decided to build his own platform instead.

Then he joined a hackathon and basically “solved” animations (this was a couple of months back). He won the hackathon. That’s when I realized this was the perfect startup idea according to my philosophy: copy something that works really well, but make it yours—change it somehow—and you’ll probably reach at least 50% of its success.  
So I asked: How can I be part of this? And now I am.

A couple of months later, [Dreamforge.ai](http://Dreamforge.ai) is live and breathing. Jonas is working on it full-time. I’m on parental leave (Sweden), so I’m putting in a solid \~6 hours a day while the baby sleeps. Another (not yet official) super-intelligent human is also joining in.

Our goal is to create the **best AI game dev experience out there**, with a strong focus on quality over quantity. We’ll listen very closely to everyone who reaches out with feedback, and we’ll iterate on that feedback at lightning speed.

So please feel free to test it out and join our Discord. Let’s get this community going! 🚀

replies.author: thelionskywalker
replies.body:
Totally fair point — and honestly, you’re not wrong in spirit.

We’re not claiming to have invented new foundation models or to be *the* AI. Under the hood, we do rely on existing models, just like basically every AI product out there right now. What we’re trying to do is remove a lot of the glue work and friction around game creation: wiring systems together, keeping state consistent, handling assets, iteration loops, and making sure “idea → playable game” actually happens instead of stalling halfway.

For some people, especially strong engineers, using a raw AI coder directly will absolutely make sense — and they’ll probably move faster that way. Dreamforge isn’t meant to replace that. It’s meant for people who want to stay at the level of game design and experimentation, and not spend mental energy on setup, structure, or babysitting the code.

If we only ever save an hour, we’ve failed. The goal is to compound that time saving across iterations and make it easier to keep going, not to pretend we’re something we’re not. Totally appreciate the skepticism though — it’s a healthy take, and we expect to earn trust over time rather than argue for it.

2. "solved animations", what does that even mean. "During a hackathon", ah ok so he didn't.

Idk if it is interesting but here is some more color on those things:  
  
My friend was called Steve jobs of summer interns by CEO Sebastian Siemankowski at Klarna when he started there. I think that is pretty cool so thats why I wrote it.

Solved animation means that at that point when the hackathon happened, there was no tool out there to animate assets. He built one and won the hackathon hosted by tech europe. If he would have gone on and published the work he would have been first but he kept on going to build dreamforge.ai.
